title: Meet Nero d'Avola
subtitle: Sicily's black grape
objectives: Describe Nero d'Avola's flavours and structure

steps.title: Dark and juicy
steps.body: Nero d'Avola means the black of Avola, a town in south-east Sicily. It gives deeply coloured wines with black cherry, plum, mulberry and sometimes chocolate and liquorice. Tannins are moderate and soft; acidity is surprisingly fresh for a hot-climate grape. It's Sicily's most planted red.

steps.title: Why it stays fresh
steps.body: Nero d'Avola keeps good natural acidity even in Sicily's heat, partly because of its genetics and partly because the best vineyards benefit from sea breezes and altitude. It's also called Calabrese, a name that may mean it came from Calabria, or from an old Sicilian dialect word. It was once shipped north to deepen paler wines.

steps.explanation: Avola is a town in south-east Sicily, the grape's historic home.

steps.title: Spotting it
steps.body: In the glass, look for deep ruby-purple colour, ripe dark fruit, and a juicy, fresh palate with soft tannins. Unoaked versions are fruity and bright; oaked ones show vanilla and spice. The juiciness and freshness, despite the ripe fruit, are the clue.

steps.prompt: Nero d'Avola was once shipped north to add colour to paler wines.
steps.explanation: Yes. Its deep colour made it a popular blending wine before it became known in its own right.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Nero d'Avola gives dark, ripe fruit with fresh acidity
Its name means the black of Avola; it's also called Calabrese
It's Sicily's most planted red grape
